analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance plans that cover other prescriptions to cover prescription contraception equally.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 129 cosponsors from both parties but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died in a House subcommittee when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred group health plans and insurers from covering prescription drugs and outpatient services while excluding prescription contraceptives and contraceptive services. It also banned plans from denying enrollment because someone might use contraception, from paying people to accept weaker coverage, and from penalizing doctors who prescribe contraception. The same rules would have applied to individual-market insurance, taking effect for plan years starting January 1, 1998.
analysis.who_benefits: Women of childbearing age with private insurance, and their families. The bill's own findings state that most women rely on employer-related insurance, that many plans covered other prescription drugs but excluded contraceptives, and that women of reproductive age spend 68% more out of pocket on health care than men, with contraception a major part of the difference.

how_it_helps.text: Plans covering other outpatient prescription drugs and devices could no longer exclude prescription contraceptive drugs and devices, with cost-sharing no higher than for other prescriptions [S2] [S3].
Plans could no longer deny or drop coverage because of a person's use or potential use of contraception, and could not offer cash rebates to get people to accept weaker protections [S3].
Doctors could not be paid less, or offered incentives, for prescribing or withholding contraception [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings cite research that contraception reduces unintended pregnancy (about 60% of pregnancies then), lowers abortion and infant mortality, and saves $4 to $14 in public costs per $1 spent [S3].
States could keep or adopt stronger protections, since the federal rules were a floor, not a ceiling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers that sponsor group plans would bear the added cost of covering contraception, which would likely be reflected in premiums. Insurers would also lose the ability to design plans around this exclusion.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and group plan sponsors

drawbacks.text: A federal coverage mandate raises plan costs, and the expense would generally be passed through to employers and into premiums, touching every covered plan rather than only the women who use contraception [S3].

The requirement is parity-based, not absolute: a plan that covers no prescription drugs or outpatient services at all would not have to cover contraception, so the weakest plans would remain exempt [S3].
The bill contains no conscience or religious exemption for employers or plan sponsors that object to contraception, a point of genuine dispute for any contraceptive-coverage mandate [S3].
Employers and insurers generally oppose federal benefit mandates as limits on plan design flexibility, and that objection was the practical obstacle the bill faced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and targeted: ending a common exclusion that made prescription contraception uniquely out of pocket for insured women, a group the bill found spent 68% more out of pocket than men. The costs are a modest, broadly spread premium increase, and the bill's own findings argue contraceptive coverage is cost-saving overall. The parity design is narrower than a full mandate but honest about it. On balance the benefits substantially outweigh the costs; the serious objections are the mandate's cost pass-through and the absence of a conscience exemption.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to a Commerce subcommittee, where it sat for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and expired in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. James Greenwood introduced the bill on July 16, 1997, joined by ten original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Marge Roukema-side colleagues such as Susan Molinari, Christopher Shays, and Constance Morella alongside Democrats Nita Lowey and Henry Waxman [S3].
The Speaker referred it to two committees at once, Education and the Workforce and Commerce, splitting jurisdiction [S1] [S5].
On July 22, 1997 it was referred to the Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Health and Environment; no further action of any kind appears for the rest of the Congress [S5].
It accumulated 129 cosponsors, 114 Democrats, 14 Republicans, and 1 Independent, but never received a committee vote or a floor vote [S4].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and unreported bills die with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group plans came out ahead: they kept the freedom to exclude prescription contraception from coverage, and the roughly 68% out-of-pocket gap women carried for reproductive health care remained in place for this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers keeping plan design freedom

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was strongly bipartisan in raw numbers, 129 cosponsors split 114 Democrats, 14 Republicans, and 1 Independent, though Republican support was a small share of the majority party, and the committees that buried the bill were all chaired by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill's findings show most insurers covered other prescription drugs but excluded prescription contraceptives, meaning the exclusion was a source of saved cost at women's expense. The bill would have ended that practice and prohibited related tactics like denying enrollment or rebating people into weaker coverage.

Employers would face somewhat higher premiums from expanded coverage, but their employees would gain a benefit directly. Because most women of childbearing age get coverage through an employer, the cost and the benefit fall on the same relationship.

Requiring plans that cover other prescriptions to cover FDA-approved contraceptives would expand the insured market for these products. That gain runs alongside the benefit to the women buying the coverage.
